title: Strong eigenstate thermalization in Singer-cycle Clifford circuits
problem: The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis explains why an isolated quantum system relaxes: each energy eigenstate already looks thermal to local observables. Its weak form, where almost every eigenstate is thermal, can hold even in integrable systems, so it does not separate systems that thermalize from systems that do not. The strong form allows no exception, and it is the one that guarantees thermalization from every initial state. Circuits built from linear feedback shift registers come close, but the product states \(\ket{0}^{\otimes L}\) and \(\ket{+}^{\otimes L}\) survive in them as nonthermal eigenstates. Is there an explicit many-body model whose eigenstates are provably all thermal?
result: A family of brickwork Clifford circuits on \(L\) qubits, for every \(L\ge2\), in which every Floquet eigenstate is thermal at infinite temperature. One period acts on Pauli strings as a Singer cycle, so each non-identity string runs through all \(2^L+1\) members of its orbit before returning. With \(D=2^L\), every matrix element of a non-identity Pauli string between two eigenstates, diagonal or not, has size at most \(2\sqrt D/(D+1)\). For an observable on a fixed number of sites the deviation from its infinite-temperature value is therefore \(O(D^{-1/2})\), uniformly in the eigenstates. The time-averaged squared fluctuation is \(O(D^{-1/2})\) from any initial state, pure or mixed.
significance: Rigorous strong-form results for concrete many-body models are rare, and this one is uniform, explicit and exponentially sharp. It separates two questions that are usually discussed together. The eigenphases are equally spaced, with one gap, so the spectrum has none of the random-matrix statistics associated with chaos, and the circuit is Clifford, hence easy to simulate from stabilizer states. Thermal eigenstates need neither. The proof method, which turns squared matrix elements into character sums over a finite field, avoids writing down the eigenstates at all.
limitations: The gate pattern is chosen separately for each size and breaks translation invariance, with no simple rule; the paper lists patterns up to \(L=18\) found by search, with at most two CNOT gates in the bulk. There is no conserved energy, so only the infinite-temperature statement is meaningful. The dynamics returns exactly after \(2^L+1\) periods, and from a stabilizer state every Pauli expectation value is \(0\) or \(\pm1\) at each step. Thermalization here means that the nonzero times are exponentially rare, not that values drift smoothly to zero. It is a single-author paper. The author states that OpenAI "chatGPT-6 Astra" supported the mathematical proofs, the code for the numerical search and the revision of the manuscript, and that all outputs were reviewed and independently verified.

III.4), the finite-field phase convention, the character-sum proof (Eqs. 125–194) and the temporal-fluctuation bound (Eqs. 195–223). Editorial checks: the circuits with the listed coefficients were built exactly for L = 2 to 8. All nonzero Pauli orbits have length 2^L+1 and there are 2^L−1 of them; the eigenphase gaps are equal except for one double gap; and the largest matrix element over all orbits and all pairs of eigenstates is 0.761, 0.619, 0.4686, 0.34245, 0.24608, 0.17539 and 0.12451, against bounds 0.800, 0.629, 0.4706, 0.34284, 0.24615, 0.17541 and 0.12451. For L up to 6 the time-averaged squared Pauli expectation from the all-zero state stays below the bound of Eq. (213). The eigenstates' second stabilizer Rényi entropy was computed for L = 3 to 7 (editorial, not in the paper).

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: The circuit has three ingredients. In the bulk, each gate on neighbouring qubits is a SWAP, or a SWAP combined with a CNOT, selected by a bit \(a_i\). At the right end sits the single-qubit gate \(SH\), a Hadamard followed by a phase gate. One Floquet period applies the odd-position gates and then the even-position gates. Every gate is Clifford, so the period maps a Pauli string to a Pauli string up to a phase. A string is labelled by \(2L\) bits, and the labels transform by a \(2L\times2L\) symplectic matrix \(M\) over the two-element field.

The closest predecessor, by Ippoliti and Long, used only SWAP and CNOT gates. That circuit permutes computational-basis states, so its eigenstates can be written down, and all but a two-dimensional eigenspace are thermal. The exceptional space is spanned by \(\ket{0}^{\otimes L}\) and \(\ket{+}^{\otimes L}\). It survives because pure-\(X\) strings and pure-\(Z\) strings never mix. The gate \(SH\) at the end of the chain mixes them, at the price that eigenstates can no longer be read off from orbits of bit strings.

The bits \(a_i\) enter only through the characteristic polynomial of \(M\), \[p_L(t)=t^{2L}+1+\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}a_i\,(t^{i}+t^{2L-i})+a_Lt^{L}.\] They are chosen so that \(p_L\) is irreducible over the two-element field and its roots have multiplicative order \(D+1\), the largest value a polynomial of this palindromic form allows. Such a choice exists for every \(L\). Irreducibility forces \(a_L=1\) and leaves no proper subspace of labels invariant. In particular no eigenstate can be a stabilizer state, because its stabilizer labels would form an invariant subspace.

Two consequences follow quickly. After \(N=D+1\) periods the circuit is the identity up to a phase, and the operators commuting with it span exactly \(D\) dimensions, so its \(D\) eigenphases are distinct. They are \(N\)-th roots of unity with a single one missing. The main theorem then bounds \(|\langle\psi_k|P|\psi_{k'}\rangle|\) for every non-identity Pauli string. An observable supported on \(\ell\) sites inherits the bound with the extra factor \(\sqrt{4^\ell-1}\) times its operator norm. The paper asks for translation-invariant models with the same property, and for models with less rigid spectra.

Our own checks add a small observation. The bound is almost reached already at moderate size, 0.12451 at \(L=8\) to five digits. The second stabilizer Rényi entropy of the eigenstates, which measures how far they are from stabilizer states, was the same for all of them to the digits computed, for example 5.437 at \(L=7\), where no state exceeds 6.011. The main theorem alone implies that it is at least about \(L-\log_25\). So a Clifford circuit, which maps stabilizer states to stabilizer states, has eigenstates that are almost as far from stabilizer states as this measure allows.

methods.technique: Squared matrix elements as finite-field character sums
methods.explanation: The eigenstates are unknown, but the projector onto each of them is a Fourier sum over powers of the circuit. A squared matrix element then becomes a double sum of traces. Each trace is a sign that can be computed exactly because Pauli labels, under the dynamics, behave like elements of a finite field that are multiplied by a fixed root. A change of variables turns the double sum into a single character sum, to which a classical bound of Weil applies.
math: Identify the labels with the field \(\mathbb F_{D^2}\) so that one period multiplies a label by \(\zeta\), with \(\zeta^{D+1}=1\). Let \(T\) be the group of powers of \(\zeta\) and \(U_s=U^n\) for \(s=\zeta^n\). The eigenstates carry the nontrivial characters \(\chi\) of \(T\), so \(\Pi_\chi=N^{-1}\sum_s\overline{\chi(s)}\,U_s\) and \[|\langle\chi|P(v)|\chi'\rangle|^2=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{s,t\in T}\overline{\chi(s)}\,\overline{\chi'(t)}\;K_v(s,t),\qquad K_v(s,t)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl[U_sP(v)U_tP(v)^\dagger\bigr].\]

The kernel is computed without any eigenstate. Moving \(U_t\) through \(P(v)\) leaves a trace of one power of \(U\) times one Pauli string, which is proportional to \(\operatorname{tr}U_{st}=-1\) when \(st\ne1\). The proportionality factor is a fourth root of unity. Because \(K_v\) is constant along an orbit of odd length \(N\), its \(N\)-th power, in which the gate-dependent phases cancel, already fixes it. The result is \[K_v(s,t)=-\psi\Bigl(v\bar v\,\bigl[1+\tfrac{s+t}{st+1}\bigr]\Bigr)\quad(st\ne1),\] with \(\bar v=v^D\) and \(\psi(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}x}\) on \(\mathbb F_D\). Also \(K_v=D\) at \(s=t=1\), and \(K_v=0\) for other pairs with \(st=1\).

The substitution \(x=(s+1)/(st+1)\) is a bijection from the pairs with \(s,t,st\ne1\) onto \(\mathbb F_{D^2}\setminus\mathbb F_D\). It satisfies \(\bar x=tx\) and \(x+\bar x=1+(s+t)/(st+1)\). Both characters become one multiplicative character \(\rho\) of a polynomial in \(x\), and \[|\langle\psi_k|P(v)|\psi_{k'}\rangle|^2=\frac{2D-Y_{k,k'}(v)}{(D+1)^2},\] \[Y_{k,k'}(v)=\sum_{x\ne0,1}\rho\bigl((x+1)^{k(D-1)}x^{-k'(D-1)}\bigr)\,(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(v\bar vx)}.\] The polynomial has two distinct roots and the additive part has degree one, so Weil's bound gives \(|Y|\le2\sqrt{D^2}=2D\). Hence the squared element is at most \(4D/(D+1)^2\).

Two consistency remarks (editorial). Summing the squared elements over \(k'\) must give 1, so their average is \(1/D\), and the theorem says that no element exceeds its average by more than a factor of four. With every \(|\langle P\rangle|^2\le4D/(D+1)^2\) and \(\sum_P\langle P\rangle^2=D\), the fourth moments obey \(\sum_P\langle P\rangle^4\le1+4D(D-1)/(D+1)^2<5\). The second stabilizer Rényi entropy \(-\log_2[D^{-1}\sum_P\langle P\rangle^4]\) is therefore larger than \(L-\log_25\).
methods.transfer: The pattern applies to any unitary of finite order whose action on an operator basis is a permutation with long cycles: replace eigenprojectors by group averages, compute traces of group elements, and look for an algebraic structure that makes the resulting sum a known exponential sum. Candidates are Clifford cellular automata, qudit circuits over odd primes, and permutation circuits. The method needs a cyclic action on labels whose orbits fill a large share of the space; it says nothing about generic Hamiltonians.

methods.technique: Temporal fluctuations from purity and a Kloosterman sum
methods.explanation: Knowing that time averages are thermal is not enough, since an expectation value could keep swinging between \(+1\) and \(-1\). The paper bounds the average of its square. For a pure state the squared Pauli coefficients equal their own symplectic Fourier transform. That identity converts the time average into a sum of signs along an orbit, which is again an exponential sum with square-root cancellation.
math: Let \(r_v=\operatorname{tr}[\rho P(v)]\). Over a full period the time-averaged square is an orbit average, \(\overline{|\langle P(v)\rangle_t|^2}=N^{-1}\sum_{s\in T}|r_{sv}|^2\). For a pure state, \(|r_v|^2=\operatorname{tr}[\rho P(v)\rho P(v)^\dagger]\). Expanding both copies of \(\rho\) in Pauli strings gives \[|r_v|^2=\frac1D\sum_w|r_w|^2(-1)^{J(v,w)},\qquad \sum_w|r_w|^2=D,\] where \(J\) is 0 or 1 according to whether the two strings commute or anticommute.

Insert this in the orbit average and separate \(w=0\): \[\overline{|\langle P(v)\rangle_t|^2}=\frac1D+\frac1{ND}\sum_{w\ne0}|r_w|^2\sum_{s\in T}(-1)^{J(sv,w)}.\] In the field description the inner sum runs over the elements of fixed norm, and it equals minus a Kloosterman sum over \(\mathbb F_D\). The reason is a count: the polynomial \(t^2+bt+c\) has its two roots either in \(\mathbb F_D\) or in conjugate positions outside it. The Weil bound for Kloosterman sums is \(2\sqrt D\), so \[\overline{|\langle P(v)\rangle_t|^2}\le\frac1D+\frac{2(D-1)}{(D+1)\sqrt D}.\]

Mixed states follow by convexity, and an observable on \(\ell\) sites by Cauchy–Schwarz with the factor \((4^\ell-1)\|O\|^2\). Taking an eigenstate as the initial state recovers strong eigenstate thermalization with the weaker rate \(D^{-1/4}\). For a stabilizer state the statement is about counting (editorial): the expectation values are \(0\) or \(\pm1\), so the bound says that the fraction of time steps with a nonzero value is at most of order \(2/\sqrt D\).
methods.transfer: The self-duality of squared Pauli coefficients for pure states is a general tool. It turns any average of \(|\langle P\rangle|^2\) over a set of strings into a question about how evenly that set splits into commuting and anticommuting parts relative to other strings. The same step appears in shadow tomography, in scrambling diagnostics and in bounds on stabilizer testing. It requires purity, and the exponential-sum estimate has to be replaced by whatever counting the set allows.
